At that time, this discussion arose among five kings, headed by King Pasenadi, who were provided with, endowed with, and indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasure: “What, indeed, is the foremost of sensual pleasures?” Some said: “Forms are the foremost of sensual pleasures.” Some said: “Sounds are the foremost of sensual pleasures.” Some said: “Odors are the foremost of sensual pleasures.” Some said: “Tastes are the foremost of sensual pleasures.” Some said: “Tactile objects are the foremost of sensual pleasures.” Since those kings were unable to persuade one another,

Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo te rājāno etadavoca – “āyāma, mārisā, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamissāma; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ etamatthaṃ paṭipucchissāma. Yathā no bhagavā byākarissati tathā naṃ dhāressāmā”ti dhāreyyāmāti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). “Evaṃ, mārisā”ti kho te rājāno rañño pasenadissa kosalassa paccassosuṃ.

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala said to those kings: “Come, sirs, let us go to the Blessed One. Having gone, we will ask the Blessed One about this matter. As the Blessed One explains it to us, so we will bear it in mind.” “So be it, sir,” those kings replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala.

Atha kho te pañca rājāno pasenadipamukhā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca [T 1.0117] – “idha, bhante, amhākaṃ pañcannaṃ rājūnaṃ pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitānaṃ samaṅgībhūtānaṃ paricārayamānānaṃ ayamantarākathā udapādi – ‘kiṃ nu kho kāmānaṃ agga’nti? Ekacce evamāhaṃsu – ‘rūpā kāmānaṃ agga’nti. Ekacce evamāhaṃsu – ‘saddā kāmānaṃ agga’nti. Ekacce evamāhaṃsu – ‘gandhā kāmānaṃ agga’nti. Ekacce evamāhaṃsu – ‘rasā kāmānaṃ agga’nti. Ekacce evamāhaṃsu – ‘phoṭṭhabbā kāmānaṃ agga’nti. Kiṃ nu kho, bhante, kāmānaṃ agga”nti?

Then those five kings, headed by King Pasenadi, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said to the Blessed One: “Here, venerable sir, while we five kings, provided with, endowed with, and indulging in the five strands of sensual pleasure, were together, this discussion arose among us: ‘What, indeed, is the foremost of sensual pleasures?’ Some said: ‘Forms are the foremost of sensual pleasures.’ Some said: ‘Sounds are the foremost of sensual pleasures.’ Some said: ‘Odors are the foremost of sensual pleasures.’ Some said: ‘Tastes are the foremost of sensual pleasures.’ Some said: ‘Tactile objects are the foremost of sensual pleasures.’ What, venerable sir, is the foremost of sensual pleasures?”

“Manāpapariyantaṃ khvāhaṃ, mahārāja, pañcasu kāmaguṇesu agganti vadāmi. Teva te ca (sī. pī. ka.), ye ca (syā. kaṃ.), mahārāja, rūpā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva te ca (sī. pī. ka.) rūpā ekaccassa amanāpā honti. Yehi ca yo rūpehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi rūpehi aññaṃ rūpaṃ uttaritaraṃ vā paṇītataraṃ vā na pattheti. Te tassa rūpā paramā honti. Te tassa rūpā anuttarā honti.

“Great king, I say that among the five strands of sensual pleasure, the foremost is that which ends in what is agreeable. Great king, those very same forms are agreeable to one person, and those same forms are disagreeable to another. A person who is pleased and whose intention is fulfilled by certain forms does not long for any other form that is higher or more excellent. For that person, those forms are supreme. For that person, those forms are unsurpassed.”

“Teva[V 1.0098], mahārāja, saddā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva saddā ekaccassa amanāpā honti. Yehi ca yo saddehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi saddehi aññaṃ saddaṃ uttaritaraṃ vā [M 1.0081] paṇītataraṃ vā na pattheti. Te tassa saddā paramā honti. Te tassa saddā anuttarā honti.

“Great king, those very same sounds are agreeable to one person, and those same sounds are disagreeable to another. A person who is pleased and whose intention is fulfilled by certain sounds does not long for any other sound that is higher or more excellent. For that person, those sounds are supreme. For that person, those sounds are unsurpassed.”

“Teva, mahārāja, gandhā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva gandhā ekaccassa amanāpā honti. Yehi ca yo gandhehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi gandhehi aññaṃ gandhaṃ uttaritaraṃ vā paṇītataraṃ vā na pattheti. Te tassa gandhā paramā honti. Te tassa gandhā anuttarā honti.

“Great king, those very same odors are agreeable to one person, and those same odors are disagreeable to another. A person who is pleased and whose intention is fulfilled by certain odors does not long for any other odor that is higher or more excellent. For that person, those odors are supreme. For that person, those odors are unsurpassed.”

“Teva, mahārāja, rasā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva rasā ekaccassa amanāpā honti. Yehi ca yo rasehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi rasehi aññaṃ rasaṃ uttaritaraṃ vā paṇītataraṃ vā na pattheti. Te tassa rasā paramā honti. Te tassa rasā anuttarā honti.

“Great king, those very same tastes are agreeable to one person, and those same tastes are disagreeable to another. A person who is pleased and whose intention is fulfilled by certain tastes does not long for any other taste that is higher or more excellent. For that person, those tastes are supreme. For that person, those tastes are unsurpassed.”

“Teva, mahārāja, phoṭṭhabbā ekaccassa manāpā honti, teva phoṭṭhabbā ekaccassa amanāpā honti. Yehi [P 1.0081] ca yo phoṭṭhabbehi attamano hoti paripuṇṇasaṅkappo, so tehi phoṭṭhabbehi aññaṃ phoṭṭhabbaṃ uttaritaraṃ vā paṇītataraṃ vā na pattheti. Te tassa [T 1.0118] phoṭṭhabbā paramā honti. Te tassa phoṭṭhabbā anuttarā hontī”ti.

“Great king, those very same tactile objects are agreeable to one person, and those same tactile objects are disagreeable to another. A person who is pleased and whose intention is fulfilled by certain tactile objects does not long for any other tactile object that is higher or more excellent. For that person, those tactile objects are supreme. For that person, those tactile objects are unsurpassed.”

Tena kho pana samayena candanaṅgaliko upāsako tassaṃ parisāyaṃ nisinno hoti. Atha kho candanaṅgaliko upāsako uṭṭhāyāsanā ekaṃsaṃ uttarāsaṅgaṃ karitvā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “paṭibhāti maṃ bhagavā, paṭibhāti maṃ sugatā”ti. “Paṭibhātu taṃ candanaṅgalikā”ti bhagavā avoca.

At that time, the lay follower Candanaṅgalika was seated in that assembly. Then the lay follower Candanaṅgalika rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and, extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, said to him: “Something occurs to me, Blessed One; something occurs to me, Sugata!” “Let it occur to you, Candanaṅgalika,” the Blessed One said.

Atha kho candanaṅgaliko upāsako bhagavato sammukhā tadanurūpāya gāthāya abhitthavi –

Then the lay follower Candanaṅgalika, in the presence of the Blessed One, praised him with a suitable verse:

“Padumaṃ [V 1.0099] yathā kokanadaṃ sugandhaṃ,

Pāto siyā phullamavītagandhaṃ;

Aṅgīrasaṃ passa virocamānaṃ,

Tapantamādiccamivantalikkhe”ti.

“Just as a fragrant red lotus, the kokanada, might be in full bloom in the morning, its fragrance undiminished; so behold Aṅgīrasa, shining, like the sun blazing in the sky.”

Atha [M 1.0082] kho te pañca rājāno candanaṅgalikaṃ upāsakaṃ pañcahi uttarāsaṅgehi acchādesuṃ. Atha kho candanaṅgaliko upāsako tehi pañcahi uttarāsaṅgehi bhagavantaṃ acchādesīti.

Then those five kings presented the lay follower Candanaṅgalika with five upper robes. Then the lay follower Candanaṅgalika presented the Blessed One with those five upper robes.

3. Doṇapākasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on the Doṇa-Measure

124. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Tena kho pana samayena rājā pasenadi kosalo doṇapākakuraṃ doṇapākasudaṃ (sī.), doṇapākaṃ sudaṃ (pī.) bhuñjati. Atha kho rājā pasenadi [T 1.0119] kosalo bhuttāvī mahassāsī yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi.

124. At Sāvatthī. At that time, King Pasenadi of Kosala was eating a doṇa-measure of cooked rice with its accompanying curry. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having eaten and breathing heavily, approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.

Atha kho bhagavā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ bhuttāviṃ mahassāsiṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi –

Then the Blessed One, knowing that King Pasenadi of Kosala had eaten and was breathing heavily, at that time recited this verse:

“Manujassa sadā satīmato,

Mattaṃ jānato laddhabhojane;

Tanukassa tanu tassa (sī. pī.) bhavanti vedanā,

Saṇikaṃ jīrati āyupālaya”nti.

“For a person who is ever mindful, knowing moderation in the food obtained, their afflictions become slight; protecting their life-span, it digests gently.”

Tena [P 1.0082] kho pana samayena sudassano māṇavo rañño pasenadissa kosalassa piṭṭhito ṭhito hoti. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo sudassanaṃ māṇavaṃ āmantesi – “ehi tvaṃ, tāta sudassana, bhagavato santike imaṃ gāthaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā mama bhattābhihāre (bhattābhihāre) ( ) sī. syā. kaṃ. pī. potthakesu natthi bhāsa. Ahañca te devasikaṃ kahāpaṇasataṃ (kahāpaṇasataṃ) ( ) sī. syā. kaṃ. potthakesu natthi niccaṃ bhikkhaṃ pavattayissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ devā”ti kho sudassano māṇavo rañño pasenadissa kosalassa paṭissutvā bhagavato santike imaṃ gāthaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā rañño pasenadissa kosalassa bhattābhihāre sudaṃ bhāsati –

At that time, the young man Sudassana was standing behind King Pasenadi of Kosala. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala addressed the young man Sudassana: “Come, dear Sudassana, learn this verse in the presence of the Blessed One and recite it each time at my meal. And I will provide for you a daily allowance of one hundred kahāpaṇas as a regular stipend.” “Very well, Your Majesty,” the young man Sudassana replied to King Pasenadi of Kosala. Having assented, he learned this verse in the presence of the Blessed One and then recited it each time at King Pasenadi of Kosala’s meal:

“Manujassa [V 1.0100] sadā satīmato,

Mattaṃ jānato laddhabhojane;

Tanukassa [T 1.0120] bhavanti vedanā,

Saṇikaṃ jīrati āyupālaya”nti.

“For a person who is ever mindful, knowing moderation in the food obtained, their afflictions become slight; protecting their life-span, it digests gently.”

Atha [M 1.0083] kho rājā pasenadi kosalo anupubbena nāḷikodanaparamatāya nāḷikodanamattāya (ka.) saṇṭhāsi. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo aparena samayena susallikhitagatto pāṇinā gattāni anumajjanto tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi – “ubhayena vata maṃ so bhagavā atthena anukampi – diṭṭhadhammikena ceva atthena samparāyikena cā”ti.

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala gradually settled on a maximum of one nāḷikā of rice. Then, on a later occasion, King Pasenadi of Kosala, with his body well-reduced, stroking his limbs with his hand, at that time uttered this inspired utterance: “Indeed, that Blessed One has compassionately benefited me in two ways—with regard to benefit in this present life and with regard to benefit in the future life.”

4. Paṭhamasaṅgāmasuttaṃ

4. The First Discourse on Battle

125. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Atha kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ abbhuyyāsi yena kāsi. Assosi kho rājā pasenadi kosalo – “rājā kira māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā mamaṃ abbhuyyāto yena kāsī”ti. Atha [P 1.0083] kho rājā pasenadi kosalo caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ ajātasattuṃ vedehiputtaṃ paccuyyāsi yena kāsi. Atha kho rājā ca māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājā ca pasenadi kosalo saṅgāmesuṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana saṅgāme rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ parājesi. Parājito ca rājā pasenadi kosalo sakameva saṅgāmā (ka.) rājadhāniṃ sāvatthiṃ paccuyyāsi pāyāsi (sī. pī.).

125. At Sāvatthī. Then King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, having assembled a four-limbed army, marched against King Pasenadi of Kosala towards Kāsi. King Pasenadi of Kosala heard: 'It is said that King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, having assembled a four-limbed army, has marched against me towards Kāsi.' Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having assembled a four-limbed army, marched out to meet King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, towards Kāsi. Then King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, and King Pasenadi of Kosala battled. In that battle, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, defeated King Pasenadi of Kosala. And the defeated King Pasenadi of Kosala marched back to his own royal capital, Sāvatthī.

Atha [T 1.0121] kho sambahulā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ –

Then, in the morning, many monks, having put on their lower robes and taking their bowls and outer robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms-food. Having wandered for alms-food in Sāvatthī, after the meal, having returned from the alms-round, they approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One:

“Idha, bhante, rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ abbhuyyāsi yena kāsi. Assosi kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo – ‘rājā [V 1.0101] kira māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā mamaṃ abbhuyyāto yena kāsī’ti. Atha kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo [M 1.0084] caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ ajātasattuṃ vedehiputtaṃ paccuyyāsi yena kāsi. Atha kho, bhante, rājā ca māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājā ca pasenadi kosalo saṅgāmesuṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana, bhante, saṅgāme rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ parājesi. Parājito ca, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo sakameva rājadhāniṃ sāvatthiṃ paccuyyāsī”ti.

“Venerable Sir, here King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, having assembled a four-limbed army, marched against King Pasenadi of Kosala towards Kāsi. Venerable Sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala heard: ‘It is said that King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, having assembled a four-limbed army, has marched against me towards Kāsi.’ Then, Venerable Sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala, having assembled a four-limbed army, marched out to meet King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, towards Kāsi. Then, Venerable Sir, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, and King Pasenadi of Kosala battled. In that battle, Venerable Sir, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, defeated King Pasenadi of Kosala. And, Venerable Sir, the defeated King Pasenadi of Kosala marched back to his own royal capital, Sāvatthī.”

“Rājā, bhikkhave, māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto pāpamitto pāpasahāyo pāpasampavaṅko; rājā ca kho, bhikkhave, pasenadi kosalo kalyāṇamitto kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko. Ajjeva ajjatañca (sī. pī.), ajjevaṃ (syā. kaṃ.), bhikkhave[T 1.0122], rājā pasenadi kosalo imaṃ rattiṃ dukkhaṃ seti parājito”ti. Idamavoca…pe…

“Monks, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, has evil friends, evil companions, and is inclined towards evil. But, monks, King Pasenadi of Kosala has good friends, good companions, and is inclined towards good. Today, monks, King Pasenadi of Kosala, being defeated, will sleep in suffering this night.”

“Jayaṃ veraṃ pasavati, dukkhaṃ seti parājito;

Upasanto sukhaṃ seti, hitvā jayaparājaya”nti.

“The victor begets hatred; the defeated sleeps in suffering. The peaceful one sleeps in happiness, having abandoned victory and defeat.”

5. Dutiyasaṅgāmasuttaṃ

5. The Second Discourse on Battle

126. ettha “atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ ajātasattuṃ vedehiputtaṃ abbhuyyāsī”ti ādinā pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ. aṭṭhakathāyaṃ hi “abbhuyyāsīti parājaye garahappatto…pe… vuttajayakāraṇaṃ sutvā abhiuyyāsī”ti vuttaṃ Atha kho rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṃ [P 1.0084] senaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ abbhuyyāsi yena kāsi. Assosi kho rājā pasenadi kosalo – “rājā kira māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā mamaṃ abbhuyyāto yena kāsī”ti. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ ajātasattuṃ vedehiputtaṃ paccuyyāsi yena kāsi. Atha kho rājā ca māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājā ca pasenadi kosalo saṅgāmesuṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana saṅgāme rājā pasenadi kosalo rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ ajātasattuṃ vedehiputtaṃ parājesi, jīvaggāhañca naṃ aggahesi. Atha kho rañño pasenadissa kosalassa etadahosi – “kiñcāpi kho myāyaṃ [M 1.0085] rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto adubbhantassa dubbhati, atha ca pana me bhāgineyyo hoti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ rañño māgadhassa ajātasattuno vedehiputtassa sabbaṃ hatthikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ [V 1.0102] assakāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ rathakāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ [T 1.0123] pattikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā jīvantameva naṃ osajjeyya”nti ossajjeyyanti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.).

126. Then King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, having assembled a four-limbed army, marched against King Pasenadi of Kosala towards Kāsi. King Pasenadi of Kosala heard: 'It is said that King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, having assembled a four-limbed army, has marched against me towards Kāsi.' Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having assembled a four-limbed army, marched out to meet King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, towards Kāsi. Then King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, and King Pasenadi of Kosala engaged in battle. In that battle, King Pasenadi of Kosala defeated King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, and captured him alive. Then this thought occurred to King Pasenadi of Kosala: 'Although this King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, wrongs me who has done no wrong, still he is my nephew. What if I were to confiscate all his elephant corps, all his cavalry corps, all his chariot corps, and all his infantry corps, and release him while he is still alive?'

Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo rañño māgadhassa ajātasattuno vedehiputtassa sabbaṃ hatthikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ assakāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ rathakāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ pattikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā jīvantameva naṃ osajji ossaji (sī.), ossajji (syā. kaṃ. pī.).

Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, having confiscated all the elephant corps, all the cavalry corps, all the chariot corps, and all the infantry corps of King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of the Vedehī queen, released him while he was still alive.

Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pavisiṃsu. Sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkantā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ –

Then, in the morning, many monks, having put on their lower robes and taking their bowls and outer robes, entered Sāvatthī for alms-food. Having wandered for alms-food in Sāvatthī, after the meal, having returned from the alms-round, they approached the Blessed One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those monks said this to the Blessed One:

“Idha[P 1.0085], bhante, rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ abbhuyyāsi yena kāsi. Assosi kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo – ‘rājā kira māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā mamaṃ abbhuyyāto yena kāsī’ti. Atha kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo caturaṅginiṃ senaṃ sannayhitvā rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ ajātasattuṃ vedehiputtaṃ paccuyyāsi yena kāsi. Atha kho, bhante, rājā ca māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto rājā ca pasenadi kosalo saṅgāmesuṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana, bhante, saṅgāme rājā pasenadi kosalo rājānaṃ māgadhaṃ ajātasattuṃ vedehiputtaṃ parājesi, jīvaggāhañca naṃ aggahesi. Atha kho, bhante, rañño pasenadissa [T 1.0124] kosalassa etadahosi – ‘kiñcāpi kho myāyaṃ rājā māgadho ajātasattu vedehiputto adubbhantassa dubbhati, atha ca pana me bhāgineyyo hoti. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ rañño māgadhassa ajātasattuno vedehiputtassa sabbaṃ hatthikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ assakāyaṃ sabbaṃ rathakāyaṃ sabbaṃ pattikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā jīvantameva naṃ osajjeyya’”nti.

“Venerable sir, here King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of Queen Vedehī, having assembled a fourfold army, marched against King Pasenadi of Kosala, toward Kāsi. Venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala heard: ‘It is said that King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of Queen Vedehī, having assembled a fourfold army, is marching against me toward Kāsi.’ Then, venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala, having assembled a fourfold army, marched out to meet King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of Queen Vedehī, toward Kāsi. Then, venerable sir, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of Queen Vedehī, and King Pasenadi of Kosala engaged in battle. In that battle, venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala defeated King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of Queen Vedehī, and captured him alive. Then, venerable sir, this thought occurred to King Pasenadi of Kosala: ‘Although this King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of Queen Vedehī, wrongs me who has done no wrong, he is, after all, my nephew. What if I were to confiscate all his elephant corps, all his cavalry, all his chariots, and all his infantry, and then release him alive?’”

“Atha [M 1.0086] kho, bhante, rājā pasenadi kosalo rañño māgadhassa ajātasattuno vedehiputtassa sabbaṃ hatthikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ assakāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā sabbaṃ rathakāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā [V 1.0103] sabbaṃ pattikāyaṃ pariyādiyitvā jīvantameva naṃ osajjī”ti. Atha kho bhagavā etamatthaṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imā gāthāyo abhāsi –

“Then, venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala, having confiscated all the elephant corps, all the cavalry, all the chariots, and all the infantry of King Ajātasattu of Magadha, son of Queen Vedehī, released him alive.” Then the Blessed One, having understood the meaning of this, on that occasion uttered these verses:

“Vilumpateva puriso, yāvassa upakappati;

Yadā caññe vilumpanti, so vilutto viluppati vilumpati (sī. pī. ka.).

“A person plunders as long as it serves his turn; but when others plunder him, the plunderer is, in turn, plundered.

“Ṭhānañhi maññati bālo, yāva pāpaṃ na paccati;

Yadā ca paccati pāpaṃ, atha dukkhaṃ nigacchati.

“A fool considers it an opportunity, so long as their evil has not yet ripened; but when the evil ripens, then that fool comes to suffering.

“Hantā labhati labhati hantā (sī. syā. kaṃ.) hantāraṃ, jetāraṃ labhate jayaṃ;

Akkosako ca akkosaṃ, rosetārañca rosako;

Atha kammavivaṭṭena, so vilutto viluppatī”ti.

“The slayer finds a slayer; the conqueror, one who conquers; the abuser finds abuse; and the vexer, one who vexes. Then, by the turning of kamma, the plunderer is, in turn, plundered.”

6. Mallikāsuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Mallikā

127. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 1.0125][P 1.0086]. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha kho aññataro puriso yena rājā pasenadi kosalo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā rañño pasenadissa kosalassa upakaṇṇake ārocesi – “mallikā, deva, devī dhītaraṃ vijātā”ti. Evaṃ vutte, rājā pasenadi kosalo anattamano ahosi.

127. At Sāvatthī. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Then a certain man approached King Pasenadi of Kosala and informed him in his ear: “Your Majesty, Queen Mallikā has given birth to a daughter.” When this was said, King Pasenadi of Kosala was displeased.

Atha kho bhagavā rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ anattamanataṃ viditvā tāyaṃ velāyaṃ imā gāthāyo abhāsi –

Then the Blessed One, knowing that King Pasenadi of Kosala was displeased, on that occasion uttered these verses:

“Itthīpi hi ekacciyā, seyyā posa janādhipa;

Medhāvinī sīlavatī, sassudevā patibbatā.

“A woman, O lord of men, may in some cases be better than a man. Nurture her. She may be wise and virtuous, a deity to her mother-in-law, and devoted to her husband.

“Tassā [V 1.0104] yo jāyati poso, sūro hoti disampati;

Tādisā subhagiyā subhariyāputto (ka.) putto, rajjampi anusāsatī”ti.

“The son who is born to her becomes a hero, O lord of the directions. The son of such a virtuous woman may even govern the kingdom.”

7. Appamādasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Heedfulness

128. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 1.0087]. Ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “atthi nu kho, bhante, eko dhammo yo ubho atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati – diṭṭhadhammikañceva atthaṃ samparāyikañcā”ti?

128. At Sāvatthī. He sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, is there one principle that encompasses and secures both kinds of welfare—welfare in this present life and welfare in the life to come?”

“Atthi kho, mahārāja, eko dhammo yo ubho atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati – diṭṭhadhammikañceva atthaṃ samparāyikañcā”ti.

“There is indeed, Great King, one principle that encompasses and secures both kinds of welfare—welfare in this present life and welfare in the life to come.”

“Katamo [T 1.0126] pana, bhante, eko dhammo, yo ubho atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati – diṭṭhadhammikañceva atthaṃ samparāyikañcā”ti?

“But what, Venerable Sir, is that one principle that encompasses and secures both kinds of welfare—welfare in this present life and welfare in the life to come?”

“Appamādo kho, mahārāja, eko dhammo, yo ubho atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati – diṭṭhadhammikañceva atthaṃ samparāyikañcāti. Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, yāni kānici jaṅgalānaṃ jaṅgamānaṃ (sī. pī.) pāṇānaṃ padajātāni, sabbāni tāni hatthipade samodhānaṃ gacchanti, hatthipadaṃ tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati – yadidaṃ mahantattena; evameva kho, mahārāja, appamādo eko dhammo, yo ubho [P 1.0087] atthe samadhiggayha tiṭṭhati – diṭṭhadhammikañceva atthaṃ samparāyikañcā”ti. Idamavoca…pe…

“Heedfulness, Great King, is the one principle that encompasses and secures both kinds of welfare—welfare in this present life and welfare in the life to come. Just as, Great King, the footprints of all land-dwelling creatures are encompassed by an elephant’s footprint, and the elephant’s footprint is declared to be the foremost among them on account of its great size; in the very same way, Great King, heedfulness is the one principle that encompasses and secures both kinds of welfare—welfare in this present life and welfare in the life to come.”

“Āyuṃ arogiyaṃ vaṇṇaṃ, saggaṃ uccākulīnataṃ;

Ratiyo patthayantena, uḷārā aparāparā.

“For one aspiring to long life, health, beauty, heaven, high birth, and to noble, successive delights,

“Appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti, puññakiriyāsu paṇḍitā;

Appamatto ubho atthe, adhiggaṇhāti paṇḍito.

the wise praise heedfulness in deeds of merit. The heedful wise one secures both kinds of welfare:

“Diṭṭhe [V 1.0105] dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti.

the welfare in this present life and the welfare in the life to come. By the attainment of this welfare, the steadfast one is called ‘wise.’”

8. Kalyāṇamittasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on the Good Friend

129. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “idha mayhaṃ[T 1.0127], bhante, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘svākkhāto bhagavatā dhammo, so ca kho kalyāṇamittassa kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa, no pāpamittassa no pāpasahāyassa no pāpasampavaṅkassā’”ti.

129. At Sāvatthī. Having sat down to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, while I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: ‘The Dhamma has been well expounded by the Blessed One, and it is for one who has good friends, good companions, and is inclined towards the good; not for one who has bad friends, bad companions, and is inclined towards the evil.’”

“Evametaṃ, mahārāja, evametaṃ, mahārāja! Svākkhāto[M 1.0088], mahārāja, mayā dhammo. So ca kho kalyāṇamittassa kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa, no pāpamittassa no pāpasahāyassa no pāpasampavaṅkassāti.

“So it is, great king, so it is! The Dhamma has been well expounded by me, great king. And it is for one who has good friends, good companions, and is inclined towards the good; not for one who has bad friends, bad companions, and is inclined towards the evil.”

“Ekamidāhaṃ, mahārāja, samayaṃ sakkesu viharāmi nagarakaṃ nāma sakyānaṃ nigamo. Atha kho, mahārāja, ānando bhikkhu yenāhaṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā maṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho, mahārāja, ānando bhikkhu maṃ etadavoca – ‘upaḍḍhamidaṃ, bhante, brahmacariyassa – yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā kalyāṇasahāyatā kalyāṇasampavaṅkatā’”ti.

“Once, great king, I was dwelling among the Sakyans in a market town of the Sakyans named Nagaraka. Then, great king, the monk Ānanda approached where I was; having approached and paid homage to me, he sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, great king, the monk Ānanda said this to me: ‘Venerable sir, this is half of the holy life: that is, good friendship, good companionship, and devotion to the good.’”

“Evaṃ vuttāhaṃ, mahārāja, ānandaṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘mā hevaṃ, ānanda, mā hevaṃ, ānanda! Sakalameva hidaṃ, ānanda, brahmacariyaṃ – yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā [P 1.0088] kalyāṇasahāyatā kalyāṇasampavaṅkatā. Kalyāṇamittassetaṃ, ānanda, bhikkhuno pāṭikaṅkhaṃ kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāvessati ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bahulīkarissati’”.

“When this was said, great king, I said this to the monk Ānanda: ‘Not so, Ānanda! Not so, Ānanda! This is the entire holy life, Ānanda: that is, good friendship, good companionship, and devotion to the good. It is to be expected of a monk who has a good friend, a good companion, and is devoted to the good that he will develop the noble eightfold path and cultivate it frequently.’”

“Kathañca, ānanda, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko [T 1.0128] ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāveti, ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bahulīkaroti? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sammādiṭṭhiṃ bhāveti [V 1.0106] vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ, sammāsaṅkappaṃ bhāveti…pe… sammāvācaṃ bhāveti…pe… sammākammantaṃ bhāveti…pe… sammāājīvaṃ bhāveti…pe… sammāvāyāmaṃ bhāveti…pe… sammāsatiṃ bhāveti…pe… sammāsamādhiṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Evaṃ kho, ānanda, bhikkhu kalyāṇamitto kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bhāveti, ariyaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ bahulīkaroti. Tadamināpetaṃ, ānanda, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā sakalamevidaṃ brahmacariyaṃ – yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā kalyāṇasahāyatā kalyāṇasampavaṅkatā”ti.

“And how, Ānanda, does a monk who has a good friend, a good companion, and is devoted to the good develop the noble eightfold path and cultivate it frequently? Here, Ānanda, a monk develops right view, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. He develops right intention… right speech… right action… right livelihood… right effort… right mindfulness… he develops right concentration, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, maturing in relinquishment. This is how, Ānanda, a monk who has a good friend, a good companion, and is devoted to the good develops the noble eightfold path and cultivates it frequently. By this method, Ānanda, it should be understood how this is the entire holy life: that is, good friendship, good companionship, and devotion to the good.”

“Mamañhi, ānanda, kalyāṇamittaṃ āgamma jātidhammā sattā jātiyā parimuccanti, jarādhammā sattā jarāya parimuccanti, byādhidhammā sattā byādhito parimuccanti, maraṇadhammā sattā maraṇena parimuccanti, sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsadhammā sattā sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsehi parimuccanti. Iminā kho etaṃ, ānanda, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā sakalamevidaṃ [M 1.0089] brahmacariyaṃ – yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā kalyāṇasahāyatā kalyāṇasampavaṅkatā”ti.

“Indeed, Ānanda, it is by relying on me as a good friend that beings subject to birth are liberated from birth; beings subject to aging are liberated from aging; beings subject to illness are liberated from illness; beings subject to death are liberated from death; beings subject to sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are liberated from sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. By this method, Ānanda, it should be understood how this is the entire holy life: that is, good friendship, good companionship, and devotion to the good.”

“Tasmātiha te, mahārāja, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘kalyāṇamitto bhavissāmi kalyāṇasahāyo kalyāṇasampavaṅko’ti. Evañhi te[T 1.0129], mahārāja, sikkhitabbaṃ.

“Therefore, great king, you should train yourself thus: ‘I will be one who has a good friend, a good companion, and is devoted to the good.’ This is how you should train yourself, great king.”

“Kalyāṇamittassa te, mahārāja, kalyāṇasahāyassa kalyāṇasampavaṅkassa ayaṃ eko [P 1.0089] dhammo upanissāya vihātabbo – appamādo kusalesu dhammesu.

“For you, great king, who has a good friend, a good companion, and is devoted to the good, this one principle should be relied upon and abided in: heedfulness in wholesome states.”

“Appamattassa te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṃ upanissāya, itthāgārassa anuyantassa evaṃ bhavissati – ‘rājā kho appamatto viharati, appamādaṃ upanissāya. Handa, mayampi appamattā viharāma, appamādaṃ upanissāyā’”ti.

“When you, great king, dwell heedfully, relying on heedfulness, it will be thus for the harem that follows you: ‘The king, indeed, dwells heedfully, relying on heedfulness. Come, let us also dwell heedfully, relying on heedfulness.’”

“Appamattassa [V 1.0107] te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṃ upanissāya, khattiyānampi anuyantānaṃ evaṃ bhavissati – ‘rājā kho appamatto viharati appamādaṃ upanissāya. Handa, mayampi appamattā viharāma, appamādaṃ upanissāyā’”ti.

“When you, great king, dwell heedfully, relying on heedfulness, it will also be thus for the Khattiyas who follow you: ‘The king, indeed, dwells heedfully, relying on heedfulness. Come, let us also dwell heedfully, relying on heedfulness.’”

“Appamattassa te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṃ upanissāya, balakāyassapi evaṃ bhavissati – ‘rājā kho appamatto viharati appamādaṃ upanissāya. Handa, mayampi appamattā viharāma, appamādaṃ upanissāyā’”ti.

“When you, great king, dwell heedfully, relying on heedfulness, it will also be thus for your army: ‘The king, indeed, dwells heedfully, relying on heedfulness. Come, let us also dwell heedfully, relying on heedfulness.’”

“Appamattassa te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṃ upanissāya, negamajānapadassapi evaṃ bhavissati – ‘rājā kho appamatto viharati, appamādaṃ upanissāya. Handa, mayampi appamattā viharāma, appamādaṃ upanissāyā’”ti?

“When you, great king, dwell heedfully, relying on heedfulness, it will also be thus for the town and country dwellers: ‘The king, indeed, dwells heedfully, relying on heedfulness. Come, let us also dwell heedfully, relying on heedfulness.’”

“Appamattassa te, mahārāja, viharato appamādaṃ upanissāya, attāpi gutto rakkhito bhavissati – itthāgārampi guttaṃ rakkhitaṃ bhavissati, kosakoṭṭhāgārampi guttaṃ rakkhitaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Idamavoca…pe…

“When you, great king, dwell heedfully, relying on heedfulness, you yourself will be guarded and protected; your harem will be guarded and protected; and your treasury and granary will be guarded and protected.”

“Bhoge [T 1.0130] patthayamānena, uḷāre aparāpare;

Appamādaṃ pasaṃsanti, puññakiriyāsu paṇḍitā.

“The wise praise heedfulness in deeds of merit for one who desires abundant and successive enjoyments.”

“Appamatto ubho atthe, adhiggaṇhāti paṇḍito;

Diṭṭhe [M 1.0090] dhamme ca yo attho, yo cattho samparāyiko;

Atthābhisamayā dhīro, paṇḍitoti pavuccatī”ti.

“The heedful wise one grasps both benefits: the benefit that is in the present existence and the benefit that is in the future life. Because of the attainment of the benefit, the steadfast one is called a ‘paṇḍita’.”

9. Paṭhamaaputtakasuttaṃ

9. The First Discourse on the Childless

130. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo divā divassa yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “handa, kuto nu tvaṃ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divā divassā”ti?

130. At Sāvatthī. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala, at midday, approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said this to King Pasenadi of Kosala, who was seated to one side: ‘Well then, great king, from where are you coming at midday?’”

“Idha, bhante, sāvatthiyaṃ seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṅkato. Tamahaṃ aputtakaṃ sāpateyyaṃ rājantepuraṃ atiharitvā āgacchāmi. Asīti, bhante, satasahassāni hiraññasseva, ko pana [P 1.0090] vādo rūpiyassa[V 1.0108]! Tassa kho pana, bhante, seṭṭhissa gahapatissa evarūpo bhattabhogo ahosi – kaṇājakaṃ bhuñjati bilaṅgadutiyaṃ. Evarūpo vatthabhogo ahosi – sāṇaṃ dhāreti tipakkhavasanaṃ. Evarūpo yānabhogo ahosi – jajjararathakena yāti paṇṇachattakena dhāriyamānenā”ti.

“Venerable sir, here in Sāvatthī a wealthy householder has passed away. As he was without an heir, I have come after having his wealth transferred to the royal palace. Venerable sir, there were eighty hundred-thousands of gold alone, to say nothing of the silver! Yet, venerable sir, such was the consumption of food of that wealthy householder: he ate broken rice with sour gruel as the second dish. Such was his consumption of clothing: he wore a hempen garment made of three pieces. Such was his consumption of vehicles: he traveled in a dilapidated little cart with a leaf-canopy being held.”

“Evametaṃ, mahārāja, evametaṃ, mahārāja! Asappuriso kho, mahārāja, uḷāre bhoge labhitvā nevattānaṃ sukheti pīṇeti, na mātāpitaro sukheti pīṇeti, na puttadāraṃ sukheti pīṇeti, na dāsakammakaraporise [T 1.0131] sukheti pīṇeti, na mittāmacce sukheti pīṇeti, na samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti sovaggikaṃ sukhavipākaṃ saggasaṃvattanikaṃ. Tassa te bhoge evaṃ sammā aparibhuñjiyamāne aparibhuñjamāno (sabbattha) rājāno vā haranti corā vā haranti aggi vā ḍahati udakaṃ vā vahati appiyā vā dāyādā haranti. Evaṃsa te evaṃ sante (sī. pī.), mahārāja, bhogā sammā aparibhuñjiyamānā parikkhayaṃ gacchanti, no paribhogaṃ.

“So it is, great king, so it is, great king! An ignoble person, great king, having obtained excellent wealth, neither makes himself happy and pleased, nor makes his parents happy and pleased, nor his wife and children happy and pleased, nor his slaves, workers, and men happy and pleased, nor his friends and associates happy and pleased, nor does he establish for ascetics and brahmins a sublime donation, which is conducive to heaven, has a happy result, and leads to a heavenly realm. As his wealth is thus not being properly enjoyed, kings carry it off, or thieves carry it off, or fire burns it, or water carries it away, or unloved heirs carry it off. Thus, great king, his wealth, not being properly enjoyed, goes to ruin, not to enjoyment.

“Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, amanussaṭṭhāne pokkharaṇī acchodakā sītodakā sātodakā setodakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā. Taṃ jano neva hareyya na piveyya na nahāyeyya na yathāpaccayaṃ vā kareyya. Evañhi taṃ, mahārāja, udakaṃ sammā aparibhuñjiyamānaṃ aparibhuñjamānaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) parikkhayaṃ gaccheyya[M 1.0091], no paribhogaṃ. Evameva kho, mahārāja, asappuriso uḷāre bhoge labhitvā nevattānaṃ sukheti pīṇeti, na mātāpitaro sukheti pīṇeti, na puttadāraṃ sukheti pīṇeti, na dāsakammakaraporise sukheti pīṇeti, na mittāmacce sukheti pīṇeti, na samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti sovaggikaṃ sukhavipākaṃ saggasaṃvattanikaṃ. Tassa te bhoge evaṃ sammā aparibhuñjiyamāne rājāno vā haranti corā vā haranti aggi vā ḍahati udakaṃ vā vahati appiyā vā dāyādā haranti. Evaṃsa te evaṃ sante (sī. pī.), mahārāja, bhogā sammā aparibhuñjiyamānā parikkhayaṃ gacchanti, no paribhogaṃ.

“Just as, great king, in an uninhabited place there might be a pond with clear water, cool water, sweet water, white water, with good banks, and delightful. People would neither carry that water, nor drink it, nor bathe in it, nor use it for any purpose as needed. Thus, great king, that water, not being properly used, would go to ruin, not to enjoyment. In the very same way, great king, an ignoble person, having obtained excellent wealth, neither makes himself happy and pleased, nor makes his parents happy and pleased, nor his wife and children happy and pleased, nor his slaves, workers, and men happy and pleased, nor his friends and associates happy and pleased, nor does he establish for ascetics and brahmins a sublime donation, which is conducive to heaven, has a happy result, and leads to a heavenly realm. As his wealth is thus not being properly enjoyed, kings carry it off, or thieves carry it off, or fire burns it, or water carries it away, or unloved heirs carry it off. Thus, great king, his wealth, not being properly enjoyed, goes to ruin, not to enjoyment.

“Sappuriso ca kho, mahārāja, uḷāre bhoge labhitvā attānaṃ sukheti pīṇeti, mātāpitaro sukheti pīṇeti, puttadāraṃ sukheti pīṇeti, dāsakammakaraporise sukheti pīṇeti, mittāmacce sukheti pīṇeti, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti sovaggikaṃ [T 1.0132] sukhavipākaṃ saggasaṃvattanikaṃ. Tassa te bhoge evaṃ sammā paribhuñjiyamāne neva rājāno haranti[V 1.0109][P 1.0091], na corā haranti, na aggi ḍahati, na udakaṃ vahati, na appiyā dāyādā haranti. Evaṃsa te, mahārāja, bhogā sammā paribhuñjiyamānā paribhogaṃ gacchanti, no parikkhayaṃ.

“But a noble person, great king, having obtained excellent wealth, makes himself happy and pleased, makes his parents happy and pleased, makes his wife and children happy and pleased, makes his slaves, workers, and men happy and pleased, and makes his friends and associates happy and pleased. He establishes for ascetics and brahmins a sublime donation, which is conducive to heaven, has a happy result, and leads to a heavenly realm. As his wealth is thus being properly enjoyed, kings do not carry it off, nor do thieves carry it off, nor does fire burn it, nor does water carry it away, nor do unloved heirs carry it off. Thus, great king, his wealth, being properly enjoyed, goes to enjoyment, not to ruin.

“Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, gāmassa vā nigamassa vā avidūre pokkharaṇī acchodakā sītodakā sātodakā setodakā supatitthā ramaṇīyā. Tañca udakaṃ jano hareyyapi piveyyapi nahāyeyyapi yathāpaccayampi kareyya. Evañhi taṃ, mahārāja, udakaṃ sammā paribhuñjiyamānaṃ paribhogaṃ gaccheyya, no parikkhayaṃ. Evameva kho, mahārāja, sappuriso uḷāre bhoge labhitvā attānaṃ sukheti pīṇeti, mātāpitaro sukheti pīṇeti, puttadāraṃ sukheti pīṇeti, dāsakammakaraporise sukheti pīṇeti, mittāmacce sukheti pīṇeti, samaṇabrāhmaṇesu uddhaggikaṃ dakkhiṇaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti sovaggikaṃ sukhavipākaṃ saggasaṃvattanikaṃ. Tassa te bhoge evaṃ sammā paribhuñjiyamāne neva rājāno haranti, na corā haranti, na aggi ḍahati, na udakaṃ vahati, na appiyā dāyādā haranti. Evaṃsa te, mahārāja, bhogā sammā paribhuñjiyamānā paribhogaṃ gacchanti, no parikkhaya”nti.

“Just as, great king, not far from a village or a town there might be a pond with clear water, cool water, sweet water, white water, with good banks, and delightful. People might carry that water, drink it, bathe in it, and use it for any purpose as needed. Thus, great king, that water, being properly used, would go to enjoyment, not to ruin. In the very same way, great king, a noble person, having obtained excellent wealth, makes himself happy and pleased, makes his parents happy and pleased, makes his wife and children happy and pleased, makes his slaves, workers, and men happy and pleased, and makes his friends and associates happy and pleased. He establishes for ascetics and brahmins a sublime donation, which is conducive to heaven, has a happy result, and leads to a heavenly realm. As his wealth is thus being properly enjoyed, kings do not carry it off, nor do thieves carry it off, nor does fire burn it, nor does water carry it away, nor do unloved heirs carry it off. Thus, great king, his wealth, being properly enjoyed, goes to enjoyment, not to ruin.”

“Amanussaṭṭhāne [M 1.0092] udakaṃva sītaṃ,

Tadapeyyamānaṃ parisosameti;

Evaṃ dhanaṃ kāpuriso labhitvā,

Nevattanā bhuñjati no dadāti.

“Just as cool water in an uninhabited place, not being drunk, dries up; so too a vile man, having obtained wealth, neither enjoys it himself nor gives it away.

Dhīro ca viññū adhigamma bhoge,

So bhuñjati kiccakaro ca hoti;

So ñātisaṅghaṃ nisabho bharitvā,

Anindito saggamupeti ṭhāna”nti.

But the wise and discerning person, having acquired wealth, enjoys it and performs his duties. Like a bull, he supports his host of relatives; blameless, he reaches the heavenly state.”

10. Dutiyaaputtakasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse on the Heirless

131. Atha [T 1.0133] kho rājā pasenadi kosalo divā divassa yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [V 1.0110] ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “handa, kuto nu tvaṃ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divā divassā”ti?

131. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One in the middle of the day. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. The Blessed One said to King Pasenadi of Kosala, who was sitting to one side: “Well then, great king, where are you coming from in the middle of the day?”

“Idha, bhante, sāvatthiyaṃ seṭṭhi gahapati kālaṅkato. Tamahaṃ aputtakaṃ sāpateyyaṃ rājantepuraṃ atiharitvā āgacchāmi. Sataṃ, bhante, satasahassāni hiraññasseva, ko pana vādo rūpiyassa! Tassa kho pana, bhante, seṭṭhissa gahapatissa evarūpo bhattabhogo ahosi – kaṇājakaṃ bhuñjati bilaṅgadutiyaṃ. Evarūpo vatthabhogo ahosi – sāṇaṃ dhāreti tipakkhavasanaṃ[P 1.0092]. Evarūpo yānabhogo ahosi – jajjararathakena yāti paṇṇachattakena dhāriyamānenā”ti.

“Venerable sir, here in Sāvatthī a wealthy householder has died. I am coming after having conveyed his heirless property into the royal palace. There were, venerable sir, ten million in gold alone, not to speak of silver! And yet, venerable sir, such was the food that wealthy householder consumed: he ate broken rice with sour gruel as a second dish. Such was the clothing he used: he wore a hempen garment made of three pieces. Such was the vehicle he used: he went in a dilapidated little cart with a leaf parasol held over him.”

“Evametaṃ, mahārāja, evametaṃ, mahārāja! Bhūtapubbaṃ so, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati taggarasikhiṃ nāma paccekasambuddhaṃ piṇḍapātena paṭipādesi. ‘Detha samaṇassa piṇḍa’nti vatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Datvā ca pana pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosi – ‘varametaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dāsā vā kammakarā vā bhuñjeyyu’nti. Bhātu ca pana ekaputtakaṃ sāpateyyassa kāraṇā jīvitā voropesi.

“So it is, great king, so it is, great king! Once in the past, great king, that wealthy householder provided almsfood to the Paccekabuddha named Tagarasikhī. Having said, ‘Give alms to the ascetic,’ he rose from his seat and left. But after giving, he later regretted it, thinking, ‘It would have been better if slaves or workers had eaten this almsfood.’ Moreover, on account of his property, he deprived his brother’s only son of life.

“Yaṃ kho so, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati taggarasikhiṃ paccekasambuddhaṃ piṇḍapātena paṭipādesi, tassa kammassa vipākena sattakkhattuṃ sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajji. Tasseva [T 1.0134] kammassa vipākāvasesena imissāyeva sāvatthiyā [M 1.0093] sattakkhattuṃ seṭṭhittaṃ kāresi. Yaṃ kho so, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati datvā pacchā vippaṭisārī ahosi – ‘varametaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dāsā vā kammakarā vā bhuñjeyyu’nti, tassa kammassa vipākena nāssuḷārāya bhattabhogāya cittaṃ namati, nāssuḷārāya vatthabhogāya cittaṃ namati, nāssuḷārāya yānabhogāya cittaṃ namati, nāssuḷārānaṃ pañcannaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ bhogāya cittaṃ namati. Yaṃ kho so, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati bhātu ca pana ekaputtakaṃ sāpateyyassa kāraṇā jīvitā voropesi, tassa kammassa vipākena bahūni vassāni bahūni vassasatāni bahūni vassasahassāni bahūni vassasatasahassāni niraye paccittha. Tasseva kammassa vipākāvasesena idaṃ sattamaṃ aputtakaṃ sāpateyyaṃ rājakosaṃ paveseti. Tassa kho, mahārāja, seṭṭhissa gahapatissa purāṇañca puññaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ, navañca puññaṃ anupacitaṃ. Ajja pana, mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati mahāroruve niraye paccatī”ti[V 1.0111]. “Evaṃ, bhante, seṭṭhi gahapati mahāroruvaṃ nirayaṃ upapanno”ti. “Evaṃ[P 1.0093], mahārāja, seṭṭhi gahapati mahāroruvaṃ nirayaṃ upapanno”ti. Idamavoca…pe….

“Great king, because that wealthy householder provided almsfood to the Paccekabuddha Tagarasikhī, as a result of that kamma he was reborn seven times in a good destination, in the heavenly world. Due to the remaining result of that same kamma, he held the position of a wealthy householder in this very Sāvatthī seven times. Great king, because that wealthy householder, after giving, later felt regret, thinking, ‘It would have been better if slaves or workers had eaten this almsfood,’ as a result of that kamma his mind did not incline to the enjoyment of excellent food, his mind did not incline to the enjoyment of excellent clothing, his mind did not incline to the enjoyment of excellent vehicles, and his mind did not incline to the enjoyment of the five excellent strands of sensual pleasures. Great king, because that wealthy householder deprived his brother’s only son of life for the sake of property, as a result of that kamma he was tormented in hell for many years, for many hundreds of years, for many thousands of years, and for many hundreds of thousands of years. Due to the remaining result of that same kamma, this is the seventh time his heirless property has entered the royal treasury. For that wealthy householder, great king, his old merit has been exhausted, and new merit has not been accumulated. Today, great king, the wealthy householder is being tormented in the Mahāroruva hell.” “Is it so, venerable sir, that the wealthy householder has been reborn in the Mahāroruva hell?” “So it is, great king, the wealthy householder has been reborn in the Mahāroruva hell.”

“Dhaññaṃ dhanaṃ rajataṃ jātarūpaṃ, pariggahaṃ vāpi yadatthi kiñci;

Dāsā kammakarā pessā, ye cassa anujīvino.

“Grain, wealth, silver, gold, or whatever other possessions there may be; slaves, workers, servants, and his dependents.

“Sabbaṃ [T 1.0135] nādāya gantabbaṃ, sabbaṃ nikkhippagāminaṃ nikkhīpagāminaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.);

Yañca karoti kāyena, vācāya uda cetasā.

“One cannot go taking any of it; all must be left behind. But whatever one does by body, speech, or mind—

“Tañhi tassa sakaṃ hoti, tañca ādāya gacchati;

Tañcassa anugaṃ hoti, chāyāva anapāyinī.

“—that indeed is one’s own, that one takes when one goes; that follows one along like a shadow that never departs.

“Tasmā kareyya kalyāṇaṃ, nicayaṃ samparāyikaṃ;

Puññāni paralokasmiṃ, patiṭṭhā honti pāṇina”nti.

“Therefore, one should do what is good, as a store for the future life. Merits are the support for beings in the next world.”

Dutiyo vaggo.

The Second Chapter.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The Summary:

Jaṭilā pañca rājāno, doṇapākakurena ca;

Saṅgāmena dve vuttāni, mallikā dhītarā (bahūsu) dve appamādena ca;

Aputtakena dve vuttā, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

Jaṭila, the Five Kings, and Doṇapāka; two are spoken on battle; Mallikā, and two on diligence; two are spoken on the sonless one; with these the chapter is told.

3. Tatiyavaggo

3. The Third Chapter

1. Puggalasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Individuals

132. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 1.0136][V 1.0112][M 1.0094]. Atha kho rājā pasenadi kosalo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “cattārome, mahārāja, puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmiṃ. Katame cattāro? Tamotamaparāyano, tamojotiparāyano, jotitamaparāyano, jotijotiparāyano”.

132. At Sāvatthī. Then King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. The Blessed One then said to King Pasenadi of Kosala as he was sitting there: “Great king, these four individuals are found existing in the world. Which four? One from darkness bound for darkness; one from darkness bound for light; one from light bound for darkness; and one from light bound for light.”

“Kathañca, mahārāja puggalo tamotamaparāyano hoti? Idha, mahārāja, ekacco puggalo nīce kule paccājāto hoti, caṇḍālakule vā venakule veṇakule (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) vā nesādakule vā rathakārakule vā pukkusakule vā dalidde appannapānabhojane kasiravuttike[P 1.0094], yattha kasirena ghāsacchādo labbhati. So ca hoti dubbaṇṇo duddasiko okoṭimako bavhābādho bahvābādho (ka.) kāṇo vā kuṇī vā khañjo vā pakkhahato vā, na lābhī annassa pānassa vatthassa yānassa mālāgandhavilepanassa seyyāvasathapadīpeyyassa. So kāyena duccaritaṃ carati, vācāya duccaritaṃ carati, manasā duccaritaṃ carati. So kāyena duccaritaṃ caritvā vācāya duccaritaṃ caritvā manasā duccaritaṃ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati.

“And how, great king, is an individual one from darkness bound for darkness? Here, great king, a certain individual is reborn in a low family—a family of outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, cart-makers, or refuse-sweepers—one that is poor, with little food and drink, living in hardship, where food and clothing are obtained with difficulty. And he is ill-favored, unsightly, dwarfish, and very sickly—blind, or with crooked limbs, or lame, or paralyzed. He is not a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, and ointments, or of beds, dwellings, and lamps. He practices misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having practiced misconduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of downfall, in hell.

“Seyyathāpi, mahārāja[T 1.0137], puriso andhakārā vā andhakāraṃ gaccheyya, tamā vā tamaṃ gaccheyya, lohitamalā vā lohitamalaṃ gaccheyya. Tathūpamāhaṃ, mahārāja, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi. Evaṃ kho, mahārāja, puggalo tamotamaparāyano hoti.

“Just as, great king, a person might go from darkness to darkness, or from gloom to gloom, or from one bloodstain to another; I say, great king, that this individual is like that. In this way, great king, an individual is one from darkness bound for darkness.

“Kathañca, mahārāja, puggalo tamojotiparāyano hoti? Idha, mahārāja, ekacco puggalo nīce kule paccājāto hoti, caṇḍālakule vā venakule vā nesādakule vā rathakārakule vā pukkusakule vā dalidde appannapānabhojane kasiravuttike, yattha kasirena ghāsacchādo labbhati. So ca kho hoti dubbaṇṇo duddasiko [M 1.0095] okoṭimako bavhābādho, kāṇo vā [V 1.0113] kuṇī vā khañjo vā pakkhahato vā, na lābhī annassa pānassa vatthassa yānassa mālāgandhavilepanassa seyyāvasathapadīpeyyassa. So kāyena sucaritaṃ carati, vācāya sucaritaṃ carati, manasā sucaritaṃ carati. So kāyena sucaritaṃ caritvā vācāya sucaritaṃ caritvā manasā sucaritaṃ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati.

“And how, great king, is an individual one who is in darkness with a destination in light? Here, great king, a certain individual is reborn in a low family—a family of caṇḍālas, bamboo-workers, hunters, cart-makers, or refuse-sweepers—one that is poor, with little food and drink, living in hardship, where food and clothing are obtained with difficulty. And he is ugly, unsightly, deformed, and very sickly—blind, or with crooked limbs, or lame, or paralyzed. He is not a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, and ointments, or of beds, dwellings, and lamps. He practices good conduct by body, speech, and mind. Having practiced good conduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”

“Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, puriso pathaviyā vā pallaṅkaṃ āroheyya, pallaṅkā vā assapiṭṭhiṃ āroheyya, assapiṭṭhiyā vā hatthikkhandhaṃ āroheyya, hatthikkhandhā vā pāsādaṃ āroheyya. Tathūpamāhaṃ, mahārāja, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi. Evaṃ kho, mahārāja, puggalo tamojotiparāyano hoti.

“Just as, great king, a person might climb from the ground onto a couch, from a couch onto a horse’s back, from a horse’s back onto an elephant’s shoulder, or from an elephant’s shoulder onto a palace; I say, great king, that this individual is like that. In this way, great king, an individual is one who is in darkness with a destination in light.”

“Kathañca, mahārāja, puggalo jotitamaparāyano hoti? Idha[T 1.0138], mahārāja, ekacco puggalo ucce kule paccājāto hoti, khattiyamahāsālakule vā brāhmaṇamahāsālakule vā gahapatimahāsālakule vā, aḍḍhe mahaddhane mahābhoge pahūtajātarūparajate [P 1.0095] pahūtavittūpakaraṇe pahūtadhanadhaññe. So ca hoti abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko, paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato, lābhī annassa pānassa vatthassa yānassa mālāgandhavilepanassa seyyāvasathapadīpeyyassa. So kāyena duccaritaṃ carati, vācāya duccaritaṃ carati, manasā duccaritaṃ carati. So kāyena duccaritaṃ caritvā vācāya duccaritaṃ caritvā manasā duccaritaṃ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati.

“And how, great king, is an individual one who is in light with a destination in darkness? Here, great king, a certain individual is reborn in a high family—a great warrior family, a great brahmin family, or a great householder family—one that is rich, with great wealth, with great possessions, with abundant gold and silver, with abundant resources and property, and with abundant wealth and grain. And he is handsome, attractive, and pleasing, endowed with the supreme beauty of complexion. He is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, and ointments, and of beds, dwellings, and lamps. He practices misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having practiced misconduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of downfall, in hell.”

“Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, puriso pāsādā vā hatthikkhandhaṃ oroheyya, hatthikkhandhā vā assapiṭṭhiṃ oroheyya, assapiṭṭhiyā vā pallaṅkaṃ oroheyya, pallaṅkā vā pathaviṃ oroheyya, pathaviyā vā andhakāraṃ paviseyya. Tathūpamāhaṃ, mahārāja, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi. Evaṃ kho, mahārāja, puggalo jotitamaparāyano hoti.

“Just as, great king, a person might descend from a palace to an elephant’s shoulder, from an elephant’s shoulder to a horse’s back, from a horse’s back to a couch, from a couch to the ground, or from the ground enter into darkness; I say, great king, that this individual is like that. In this way, great king, an individual is one who is in light with a destination in darkness.”

“Kathañca, mahārāja, puggalo jotijotiparāyano hoti? Idha, mahārāja, ekacco puggalo ucce kule paccājāto hoti, khattiyamahāsālakule vā brāhmaṇamahāsālakule vā gahapatimahāsālakule [M 1.0096] vā, aḍḍhe mahaddhane mahābhoge pahūtajātarūparajate pahūtavittūpakaraṇe [T 1.0139] pahūtadhanadhaññe. So ca hoti abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko, paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato[V 1.0114], lābhī annassa pānassa vatthassa yānassa mālāgandhavilepanassa seyyāvasathapadīpeyyassa. So kāyena sucaritaṃ carati, vācāya sucaritaṃ carati, manasā sucaritaṃ carati. So kāyena sucaritaṃ caritvā vācāya sucaritaṃ caritvā manasā sucaritaṃ caritvā, kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati.

“And how, great king, is an individual one who is in light with a destination in light? Here, great king, a certain individual is reborn in a high family—a great warrior family, a great brahmin family, or a great householder family—one that is rich, with great wealth, with great possessions, with abundant gold and silver, with abundant resources and property, and with abundant wealth and grain. And he is handsome, attractive, and pleasing, endowed with the supreme beauty of complexion. He is a recipient of food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, and ointments, and of beds, dwellings, and lamps. He practices good conduct by body, speech, and mind. Having practiced good conduct by body, speech, and mind, with the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.”

“Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, puriso pallaṅkā vā pallaṅkaṃ saṅkameyya, assapiṭṭhiyā vā assapiṭṭhiṃ saṅkameyya, hatthikkhandhā vā hatthikkhandhaṃ saṅkameyya, pāsādā vā pāsādaṃ saṅkameyya. Tathūpamāhaṃ, mahārāja, imaṃ puggalaṃ vadāmi. Evaṃ kho, mahārāja, puggalo jotijotiparāyano hoti. Ime [P 1.0096] kho, mahārāja, cattāro puggalā santo saṃvijjamānā lokasmi”nti. Idamavoca…pe…

“Just as, great king, a person might move from one couch to another, from one horse’s back to another, from one elephant’s back to another, or from one palace to another; I say, great king, that this individual is like that. In this way, great king, an individual is one who is in light with a destination in light. Indeed, great king, these four kinds of people are found existing in the world.” The Blessed One said this…

“Daliddo puriso rāja, assaddho hoti maccharī;

Kadariyo pāpasaṅkappo, micchādiṭṭhi anādaro.

“A poor man, O king, is faithless and stingy; he is miserly, has evil intentions, holds wrong views, and is disrespectful.

“Samaṇe brāhmaṇe vāpi, aññe vāpi vanibbake;

Akkosati paribhāsati, natthiko hoti rosako.

He insults and reviles ascetics or brahmins, or other mendicants; he is a nihilist and is quarrelsome.

“Dadamānaṃ nivāreti, yācamānāna bhojanaṃ;

Tādiso puriso rāja, mīyamāno janādhipa;

Upeti nirayaṃ ghoraṃ, tamotamaparāyano.

He prevents one who is giving food to those who ask. Such a person, O king, lord of men, upon dying, goes to a terrible hell; he is one who is in darkness with a destination in darkness.

“Daliddo puriso rāja, saddho hoti amaccharī;

Dadāti [T 1.0140] seṭṭhasaṅkappo, abyaggamanaso naro.

“A poor man, O king, is faithful and not stingy; he gives with noble intentions, a man with an undistracted mind.

“Samaṇe brāhmaṇe vāpi, aññe vāpi vanibbake;

Uṭṭhāya abhivādeti, samacariyāya sikkhati.

Rising, he pays homage to ascetics or brahmins, or other mendicants, and he trains in harmonious conduct.

“Dadamānaṃ [V 1.0115] na vāreti na nivāreti (sī.), yācamānāna bhojanaṃ;

Tādiso puriso rāja, mīyamāno janādhipa;

Upeti tidivaṃ ṭhānaṃ, tamojotiparāyano.

He does not prevent one who is giving food to those who ask. Such a person, O king, lord of men, upon dying, goes to the heavenly abode; he is one who is in darkness with a destination in light.

“Aḍḍho [M 1.0097] ce aḍḍho ve (pī. ka.) puriso rāja, assaddho hoti maccharī;

Kadariyo pāpasaṅkappo, micchādiṭṭhi anādaro.

“If a man, O king, is wealthy, he is faithless and stingy; he is miserly, has evil intentions, holds wrong views, and is disrespectful.

“Samaṇe brāhmaṇe vāpi, aññe vāpi vanibbake;

Akkosati paribhāsati, natthiko hoti rosako.

He insults and reviles ascetics or brahmins, or other mendicants; he is a nihilist and is quarrelsome.

“Dadamānaṃ nivāreti, yācamānāna bhojanaṃ;

Tādiso puriso rāja, mīyamāno janādhipa;

Upeti nirayaṃ ghoraṃ, jotitamaparāyano.

He prevents one who is giving food to those who ask. Such a person, O king, lord of men, upon dying, goes to a terrible hell; he is one who is in light with a destination in darkness.

“Aḍḍho ce puriso rāja, saddho hoti amaccharī;

Dadāti seṭṭhasaṅkappo, abyaggamanaso naro.

“If a man, O king, is wealthy, he is faithful and not stingy; he gives with noble intentions, a man with an undistracted mind.

“Samaṇe brāhmaṇe vāpi, aññe vāpi vanibbake;

Uṭṭhāya abhivādeti, samacariyāya sikkhati.

Rising, he pays homage to ascetics or brahmins, or other mendicants, and he trains in harmonious conduct.

“Dadamānaṃ na vāreti, yācamānāna bhojanaṃ;

Tādiso puriso rāja, mīyamāno janādhipa;

Upeti tidivaṃ ṭhānaṃ, jotijotiparāyano”ti.

“He does not prevent one who is giving food to those who ask. Such a person, O king, lord of men, upon dying, goes to the heavenly abode; he is one who goes from light to light.”

2. Ayyikāsuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on the Grandmother

133. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 1.0141]. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ bhagavā [P 1.0097] etadavoca – “handa, kuto nu tvaṃ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divādivassā”ti?

133. At Sāvatthī. While King Pasenadi of Kosala was seated to one side, the Blessed One said to him: “Well then, great king, from where are you coming at this midday?”

“Ayyikā [V 1.0116] me, bhante, kālaṅkatā jiṇṇā vuḍḍhā mahallikā addhagatā vayoanuppattā vīsavassasatikā jātiyā. Ayyikā kho pana me, bhante, piyā hoti manāpā. Hatthiratanena cepāhaṃ, bhante, labheyyaṃ ‘mā me ayyikā kālamakāsī’ti, hatthiratanampāhaṃ dadeyyaṃ – ‘mā me ayyikā kālamakāsī’ti. Assaratanena cepāhaṃ, bhante, labheyyaṃ ‘mā me ayyikā kālamakāsī’ti, assaratanampāhaṃ dadeyyaṃ – ‘mā me ayyikā kālamakāsī’ti. Gāmavarena cepāhaṃ bhante, labheyyaṃ ‘mā me ayyikā kālamakāsī’ti, gāmavarampāhaṃ dadeyyaṃ – ‘mā me ayyikā kālamakāsī’ti. Janapadapadesena janapadena (sī. syā. pī.) cepāhaṃ, bhante, labheyyaṃ [M 1.0098] ‘mā me ayyikā kālamakāsī’ti, janapadapadesampāhaṃ dadeyyaṃ – ‘mā me ayyikā kālamakāsī’ti. ‘Sabbe sattā, mahārāja, maraṇadhammā maraṇapariyosānā maraṇaṃ anatītā’ti. ‘Acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Yāvasubhāsitamidaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā – sabbe sattā maraṇadhammā maraṇapariyosānā maraṇaṃ anatītā’”ti.

“Venerable sir, my grandmother has passed away. She was old, aged, elderly, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life—one hundred and twenty years of age. Venerable sir, my grandmother was dear and agreeable to me. If, venerable sir, I could have prevented my grandmother from dying by giving an elephant-jewel, I would have given an elephant-jewel, so that my grandmother would not die. If, venerable sir, I could have prevented my grandmother from dying by giving a horse-jewel, I would have given a horse-jewel, so that my grandmother would not die. If, venerable sir, I could have prevented my grandmother from dying by giving a choice village, I would have given a choice village, so that my grandmother would not die. If, venerable sir, I could have prevented my grandmother from dying by giving a province, I would have given a province, so that my grandmother would not die.” “All beings, great king, are of a nature to die, have death as their end, and have not gone beyond death.” “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is amazing, venerable sir! How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One: ‘All beings are of a nature to die, have death as their end, and have not gone beyond death.’”

“Evametaṃ, mahārāja, evametaṃ, mahārāja! Sabbe sattā maraṇadhammā [T 1.0142] maraṇapariyosānā maraṇaṃ anatītā. Seyyathāpi, mahārāja, yāni kānici kumbhakārabhājanāni āmakāni ceva pakkāni ca sabbāni tāni bhedanadhammāni bhedanapariyosānāni bhedanaṃ anatītāni; evameva kho, mahārāja, sabbe sattā maraṇadhammā maraṇapariyosānā maraṇaṃ anatītā”ti. Idamavoca…pe…

“So it is, great king, so it is! All beings are of a nature to die, have death as their end, and have not gone beyond death. Just as, great king, whatever potter’s vessels there are, both unbaked and baked, all are of a nature to break, have breaking as their end, and have not gone beyond breaking; even so, great king, all beings are of a nature to die, have death as their end, and have not gone beyond death.”

“Sabbe sattā marissanti, maraṇantañhi jīvitaṃ;

Yathākammaṃ gamissanti, puññapāpaphalūpagā;

Nirayaṃ pāpakammantā, puññakammā ca suggatiṃ.

“All beings will die, for life has death as its end. According to their kamma they will go, faring according to the fruit of their merit and demerit: those who have done evil deeds to hell, and those who have done meritorious deeds to a good destination.

“Tasmā kareyya kalyāṇaṃ, nicayaṃ samparāyikaṃ;

Puññāni paralokasmiṃ, patiṭṭhā honti pāṇina”nti.

“Therefore, one should do what is good, accumulating that which is for the future life. Merits are the support for living beings in the next world.”

3. Lokasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on the World

134. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[P 1.0098]. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca [V 1.0117] – “kati nu kho, bhante, lokassa dhammā uppajjamānā uppajjanti ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāyā”ti? “Tayo kho, mahārāja, lokassa dhammā uppajjamānā uppajjanti ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāya. Katame tayo? Lobho kho, mahārāja, lokassa dhammo, uppajjamāno uppajjati ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāya. Doso [T 1.0143] kho, mahārāja, lokassa dhammo, uppajjamāno uppajjati ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāya. Moho kho, mahārāja, lokassa dhammo, uppajjamāno uppajjati ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāya. Ime kho, mahārāja, tayo lokassa dhammā uppajjamānā uppajjanti ahitāya dukkhāya aphāsuvihārāyā”ti. Idamavoca…pe…

134. At Sāvatthī. Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, how many things are there that, when arising in the world, arise for harm, for suffering, and for discomfort?” “Great King, there are three things that, when arising in the world, arise for harm, for suffering, and for discomfort. What are the three? Greed, Great King, is a thing that, when arising in the world, arises for harm, for suffering, and for discomfort. Hatred, Great King, is a thing that, when arising in the world, arises for harm, for suffering, and for discomfort. Delusion, Great King, is a thing that, when arising in the world, arises for harm, for suffering, and for discomfort. These, Great King, are the three things that, when arising in the world, arise for harm, for suffering, and for discomfort.”

“Lobho [M 1.0099] doso ca moho ca, purisaṃ pāpacetasaṃ;

Hiṃsanti attasambhūtā, tacasāraṃva samphala”nti.

“Greed, hatred, and delusion, arisen from within oneself, harm the person of wicked mind, just as its own fruit destroys the reed.”

4. Issattasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Archery

135. Sāvatthinidānaṃ. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho rājā pasenadi kosalo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kattha nu kho, bhante, dānaṃ dātabba”nti? “Yattha kho, mahārāja, cittaṃ pasīdatī”ti. “Kattha pana, bhante, dinnaṃ mahapphala”nti? “Aññaṃ kho etaṃ, mahārāja, kattha dānaṃ dātabbaṃ, aññaṃ panetaṃ kattha dinnaṃ mahapphalanti? Sīlavato kho, mahārāja, dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ, no tathā dussīle. Tena hi, mahārāja, taññevettha paṭipucchissāmi. Yathā, te khameyya, tathā naṃ byākareyyāsi. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idha tyassa yuddhaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ saṅgāmo samupabyūḷho samūpabbūḷho (sī.), samupabbuḷho (pī.). Atha āgaccheyya khattiyakumāro asikkhito akatahattho akatayoggo akatūpāsano [P 1.0099] bhīru chambhī utrāsī palāyī. Bhareyyāsi taṃ purisaṃ, attho ca te tādisena purisenā”ti? “Nāhaṃ, bhante, bhareyyaṃ taṃ purisaṃ, na ca me attho tādisena purisenā”ti. “Atha āgaccheyya brāhmaṇakumāro asikkhito…pe… atha āgaccheyya vessakumāro asikkhito…pe… atha āgaccheyya suddakumāro asikkhito…pe… na ca me attho tādisena purisenā”ti.

135. At Sāvatthī. Seated to one side, King Pasenadi of Kosala said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, to whom should a gift be given?” “Great King, it should be given to whomever the mind is pleased with.” “But, Venerable Sir, a gift given to whom has great fruit?” “Great King, the question ‘To whom should a gift be given?’ is one thing, and the question ‘A gift given to whom has great fruit?’ is another. A gift given to the virtuous, Great King, has great fruit; not so a gift given to the unvirtuous. In that case, Great King, I will question you in return. You should answer as you see fit. What do you think, Great King? Suppose a battle was imminent for you, and the army was arrayed. Then a young khattiya might come—untrained, unskilled, unpracticed, unexercised, fearful, trembling, terrified, and prone to flight. Would you support that man, and would you have a need for such a man?” “No, Venerable Sir, I would not support that man, nor would I have a need for such a man.” “Then a young brahmin might come, untrained… or a young vessa might come, untrained… or a young sudda might come, untrained…” “…nor would I have a need for such a man.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idha tyassa yuddhaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ saṅgāmo samupabyūḷho. Atha āgaccheyya [V 1.0118] khattiyakumāro susikkhito katahattho katayoggo katūpāsano abhīru acchambhī anutrāsī apalāyī. Bhareyyāsi taṃ purisaṃ, attho ca te tādisena purisenā”ti? “Bhareyyāhaṃ, bhante[T 1.0144], taṃ purisaṃ, attho ca me tādisena purisenā”ti. “Atha āgaccheyya brāhmaṇakumāro…pe… atha āgaccheyya vessakumāro…pe… atha āgaccheyya suddakumāro susikkhito katahattho katayoggo katūpāsano abhīru acchambhī anutrāsī apalāyī. Bhareyyāsi taṃ purisaṃ, attho ca te tādisena purisenā”ti? “Bhareyyāhaṃ, bhante, taṃ purisaṃ, attho ca me tādisena purisenā”ti.

“What do you think, Great King? Suppose a battle was imminent for you, and the army was arrayed. Then a young khattiya might come—well-trained, skilled of hand, practiced, exercised, fearless, not trembling, not terrified, and not prone to flight. Would you support that man, and would you have a need for such a man?” “Venerable Sir, I would support that man, and I would have a need for such a man.” “Then a young brahmin might come… or a young vessa might come… or a young sudda might come—well-trained, skilled of hand, practiced, exercised, fearless, not trembling, not terrified, and not prone to flight. Would you support that man, and would you have a need for such a man?” “Venerable Sir, I would support that man, and I would have a need for such a man.”

“Evameva kho, mahārāja, yasmā kasmā cepi yasmā cepi (sī. syā. kaṃ. ka.) kulā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito hoti, so ca hoti pañcaṅgavippahīno pañcaṅgasamannāgato, tasmiṃ [M 1.0100] dinnaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti. Katamāni pañcaṅgāni pahīnāni honti? Kāmacchando pahīno hoti, byāpādo pahīno hoti, thinamiddhaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīnaṃ hoti, vicikicchā pahīnā hoti. Imāni pañcaṅgāni pahīnāni honti. Katamehi pañcahaṅgehi [T 1.0145] samannāgato hoti? Asekkhena sīlakkhandhena samannāgato hoti, asekkhena samādhikkhandhena samannāgato hoti, asekkhena paññākkhandhena samannāgato [P 1.0100] hoti, asekkhena vimuttikkhandhena samannāgato hoti, asekkhena vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhena samannāgato hoti. Imehi pañcahaṅgehi samannāgato hoti. Iti pañcaṅgavippahīne pañcaṅgasamannāgate dinnaṃ mahapphala”nti. Idamavoca bhagavā…pe… satthā –

“In just this way, Great King, from whatever family one has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, if he has abandoned five factors and is endowed with five factors, a gift given to him is of great fruit. What are the five factors that are abandoned? Sensual desire is abandoned; ill will is abandoned; sloth and torpor are abandoned; restlessness and remorse are abandoned; doubt is abandoned. These are the five factors that are abandoned. With what five factors is he endowed? He is endowed with the Arahant’s aggregate of virtue, endowed with the Arahant’s aggregate of concentration, endowed with the Arahant’s aggregate of wisdom, endowed with the Arahant’s aggregate of liberation, and endowed with the Arahant’s aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. With these five factors is he endowed. Thus, a gift given to one who has abandoned five factors and is endowed with five factors is of great fruit.” This is what the Blessed One said… the Teacher:

“Issattaṃ issatthaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.) balavīriyañca balaviriyañca (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), yasmiṃ vijjetha māṇave;

Taṃ yuddhattho bhare rājā, nāsūraṃ jātipaccayā.

“A king in need of a warrior should support a youth in whom are found archery, strength, and energy; he should not support one who is not brave on account of his birth.

“Tatheva khantisoraccaṃ, dhammā yasmiṃ patiṭṭhitā;

Ariyavuttiṃ medhāviṃ, hīnajaccampi pūjaye.

In just the same way, one should honor a wise person of noble conduct, even one of low birth, in whom the qualities of patience and gentleness are established.

“Kāraye assame ramme, vāsayettha bahussute;

Papañca vivane kayirā, dugge saṅkamanāni ca.

One should have delightful hermitages built, and settle the very learned there. One should make reservoirs in the wilderness, and bridges and paths in difficult terrain.

“Annaṃ [V 1.0119] pānaṃ khādanīyaṃ, vatthasenāsanāni ca;

Dadeyya ujubhūtesu, vippasannena cetasā.

One should give food, drink, and edibles, along with robes and lodging, to those who are upright, with a confident and serene mind.

“Yathā hi megho thanayaṃ, vijjumālī satakkaku;

Thalaṃ ninnañca pūreti, abhivassaṃ vasundharaṃ.

Just as a thundering cloud, with its garlands of lightning and a hundred peaks, fills both the high and low lands, raining down upon the earth;

“Tatheva saddho sutavā, abhisaṅkhacca bhojanaṃ;

Vanibbake tappayati, annapānena paṇḍito.

So too a wise person who has faith and is learned, having prepared a meal, satisfies the mendicants with food and drink.

“Āmodamāno pakireti, detha dethāti bhāsati;

Taṃ [T 1.0146] hissa gajjitaṃ hoti, devasseva pavassato;

Sā puññadhārā vipulā, dātāraṃ abhivassatī”ti.

Rejoicing, he gives generously, saying, ‘Give! Give!’ This is his thunder, like that of the raining cloud. That vast stream of merit rains down upon the giver.”

5. Pabbatūpamasuttaṃ

5. The Simile of the Mountain

136. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 1.0101]. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho rājānaṃ pasenadiṃ kosalaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “handa, kuto nu tvaṃ, mahārāja, āgacchasi divā divassā”ti? “Yāni tāni, bhante, raññaṃ khattiyānaṃ muddhāvasittānaṃ issariyamadamattānaṃ kāmagedhapariyuṭṭhitānaṃ janapadatthāvariyappattānaṃ mahantaṃ pathavimaṇḍalaṃ abhivijiya ajjhāvasantānaṃ rājakaraṇīyāni bhavanti, tesu khvāhaṃ, etarahi ussukkamāpanno”ti.

136. At Sāvatthī. While King Pasenadi of Kosala was sitting to one side, the Blessed One said to him: “Now, great king, from where are you coming in the middle of the day?” “Venerable sir, those royal duties of kings—anointed kṣatriyas, intoxicated with the pride of sovereignty, overcome by attachment to sensual pleasures, having attained stability in their country, and dwelling having conquered a great sphere of the earth—it is with these that I am now occupied.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mahārāja, idha te puriso āgaccheyya [P 1.0101] puratthimāya disāya saddhāyiko paccayiko. So taṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘yagghe, mahārāja, jāneyyāsi, ahaṃ āgacchāmi puratthimāya disāya. Tatthaddasaṃ mahantaṃ pabbataṃ abbhasamaṃ sabbe pāṇe nippothento āgacchati. Yaṃ te, mahārāja, karaṇīyaṃ, taṃ karohī’ti. Atha dutiyo puriso āgaccheyya pacchimāya disāya…pe… atha tatiyo puriso āgaccheyya uttarāya disāya…pe… atha catuttho puriso āgaccheyya dakkhiṇāya disāya saddhāyiko paccayiko. So taṃ [T 1.0147] upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vadeyya – ‘yagghe mahārāja, jāneyyāsi, ahaṃ āgacchāmi [V 1.0120] dakkhiṇāya disāya. Tatthaddasaṃ mahantaṃ pabbataṃ abbhasamaṃ sabbe pāṇe nippothento āgacchati. Yaṃ te, mahārāja, karaṇīyaṃ taṃ karohī’ti. Evarūpe te, mahārāja, mahati mahabbhaye samuppanne dāruṇe manussakkhaye manussakāye (ka.) dullabhe manussatte kimassa karaṇīya”nti?

“What do you think, great king? Suppose a man, whose word is to be believed and trusted, were to come to you from the eastern direction. Having approached you, he would say this: ‘If it pleases you, great king, may you know this: I am coming from the eastern direction. There I saw a great mountain, as high as the clouds, advancing and crushing all living beings to powder. Whatever is to be done by you, great king, do it.’ Then a second man were to come from the western direction… Then a third man were to come from the northern direction… Then a fourth man, whose word is to be believed and trusted, were to come from the southern direction. Having approached you, he would say this: ‘If it pleases you, great king, may you know this: I am coming from the southern direction.
